title: Prahaar: Rajkummar Rao — and a Stunning Kasab — Make the 26/11 Trial Gripping
excerpt: Critics hand the 26/11 trial drama the week's strongest notices — anchored by Rajkummar Rao's restraint and a Kasab performance reviewers call stunning.
body:
• Critics rate Prahaar 3 to 4.5 out of 5 — the warmest-reviewed Indian release of the week
  • Lalit Prabhakar's Ajmal Kasab is the breakout performance; Rajkummar Rao's restrained Ujjwal Nikam anchors the film
  • Jaideep Ahlawat's post-interval entry and the dialogue writing draw repeated praise
  • The 140-minute runtime and the personal-life track are the main reservations, echoed in cooler audience first reactions

Every Indian remembers where they were when Mumbai was attacked on 26/11. Far fewer know the story Avinash Arun's Prahaar tells: the years of legal grind that followed, as special public prosecutor Ujjwal Nikam built the case against Ajmal Kasab, the lone surviving gunman — the evidence, the arguments, the waiting. Rajkummar Rao plays Nikam in Prahaar: The Untold Story of Ujjwal Nikam, a Maddock Films courtroom drama that also reaches back to the 1993 Bombay bombings case. The early critical response is the warmest of this week's releases, and it converges on an unexpected headline: the film's most praised performance belongs not to its star, but to the man playing Kasab.

The consensus

Critic ratings run from 3 to 4.5 out of 5. IANS, at the top with 4.5, calls it a powerful performance-driven drama built on Nikam's dictum that justice hurried is justice buried; Bollywood Hungama, at 4, labels it a must-watch experience; India Forums and IWMBuzz both settle at 3.5, praising restraint and conviction; GG2, the coolest of the major notices at 3, still commends a courtroom drama that stays focused and rarely loses its balance. The disagreements are about pace outside the courtroom, not about the film's seriousness or its cast. Audience first reactions are a notch cooler than the critics — pacing is the word that recurs — but reviewers are close to united: this is a well-made, well-acted account of a trial the country mostly remembers as a headline.

What's praised

Lalit Prabhakar, as Kasab, is the revelation. GG2 calls his transformation stunningly convincing — a first-rate impersonation that little else in the film matches. Bollywood Hungama uses the same register: outstanding, unsettling and controlled, a portrayal that avoids histrionics and leaves a lasting impression. That a supporting actor playing one of the most hated men in modern Indian history walks away with the reviews tells you something about the film's confidence.

Rajkummar Rao anchors it. India Forums says he shines with restraint; IWMBuzz writes that he commands the screen so completely it stops feeling like acting, and singles out the moment Nikam rejects Kasab's claim to be a juvenile as one of the sequences that gives you goosebumps. The ensemble behind them is praised in depth: Jaideep Ahlawat, flawless as ever as the Pakistani prosecutor who enters after the interval and, per IWMBuzz, provides the film's real kick; Sikandar Kher, excellent as Kasab's defence lawyer, with a family restaurant scene Bollywood Hungama calls splendid; Ashish Vidyarthi bringing credibility as Justice Tahiliyani; and Wamiqa Gabbi making her presence count as Nikam's wife Jyoti. IWMBuzz also reserves special praise for the dialogues, and Bollywood Hungama calls the background score a major plus that raises the tension at the crucial junctures — in a film with no songs and no need of them.

What's criticized

The 140 minutes are the argument. IWMBuzz concedes the first half grips and builds well, but the detour into Nikam's personal life — the sacrifices of a man whose profession leaves little room for an ordinary family — could have been shorter. First-day audience reactions collected by Dainik Jagran make the point more sharply: powerful speeches, but a film that could have wrapped within 120 minutes, with a few viewers also noting accent wobbles in Rao's portrayal and too little for Wamiqa Gabbi to do. Trade expectations are modest — a soft opening was projected on limited pre-release marketing — which makes Prahaar a word-of-mouth film rather than an opening-weekend juggernaut.

What this means for you

For diaspora viewers, this is the critics' pick of the week: a Hindi courtroom drama about the legal aftermath of an event seared into every Indian household's memory, carried by two performances — Rao's restraint and Prabhakar's transformation — that reviewers cannot stop talking about. At 140 minutes it asks for an evening, not a background watch. If you see one Indian film in cinemas this weekend, the reviews say it should be this one.

data_cards.rating_consensus: Critics hand Prahaar the week's strongest notices: a restrained, performance-led courtroom drama whose only real fault is length — anchored by Rajkummar Rao and stolen by Lalit Prabhakar's Kasab.
